definition.text: Musical texture describes the density of a passage and the way its simultaneous voices or layers interact.

facts.text: Monophony presents one melodic line without an independent accompaniment.
Heterophony presents simultaneous variants of essentially the same melody.

anchor.quote: multiple variants of a single melodic line

facts.text: Homophony coordinates multiple voices at a shared harmonic pace, often as melody with accompaniment.
Polyphony combines voices that carry independent melodic lines and rhythms.

misconceptions.text: Students may label any passage with several performers as polyphonic.
misconceptions.corrective: Classify the relationship among lines: several performers can reinforce one monophonic line or form a homophonic melody-and-accompaniment texture.

examples.text: A listener compares a solo unaccompanied melody, a singer over block-chord accompaniment, and two independent imitative melodies.

attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

definition.text: Dynamics, articulation, and tempo are distinct performance dimensions: loudness, the attack or connection of notes, and performance speed.

facts.text: Dynamic markings communicate loudness rather than speed or note length.

anchor.quote: Dynamics indicate the loudness of music

facts.text: A crescendo increases loudness, while a decrescendo or diminuendo decreases it.
Articulation describes how notes connect or separate and how their attacks are emphasized.
Tempo indicates how fast or slowly a composition is performed and may be stated with text or beats per minute.

misconceptions.text: Students may treat a louder marking as a request to play faster.
misconceptions.corrective: Read each dimension separately: dynamics change loudness, tempo changes speed, and articulation changes connection or attack.

examples.text: A performer plays the same phrase softly, at an unchanged tempo, with staccato rather than legato articulation.

attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

definition.text: A musical phrase is a relatively complete thought directed toward a goal, and a cadence is a harmonic event that can mark its ending.

facts.text: A sentence is a phrase archetype with a presentation followed by a continuation.
A period combines an antecedent phrase with a consequent phrase.
The antecedent normally ends with a weaker cadence than the consequent.
Cadential closure is a common phrase goal in tonal classical music, but other musical styles can establish different goals.

misconceptions.text: Students may mark every pause or repeated motive as the end of a phrase.
misconceptions.corrective: Test for a larger directed unit and evidence of closure; a local pause or motive boundary alone does not establish a phrase ending.

examples.text: An analyst hears a four-measure antecedent end inconclusively and a consequent answer it with stronger closure.

attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors

definition.text: Tonicization briefly makes a non-tonic harmony sound like a tonic, while modulation establishes a longer-term change of tonic.

facts.text: A modulation may introduce the new key directly and abruptly.
A pivot-chord modulation uses a shared chord to make the move between keys more subtle.
Extended tonicization can blur the boundary between a temporary tonic and a full modulation.
The duration and structural stability of the new tonic help distinguish modulation from a momentary tonicization.

misconceptions.text: Students may call every chromatic dominant chord a key change.
misconceptions.corrective: Determine whether the music sustains and structurally confirms a new tonic; a brief applied chord can tonicize without modulating.

examples.text: An analyst compares a single applied dominant resolving immediately in the home key with a pivot chord followed by a sustained new key.

attribution: Open Music Theory by Mark Gotham, Kyle Gullings, Chelsey Hamm, Bryn Hughes, Brian Jarvis, Megan Lavengood, John Peterson, and contributors
